sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3, languoid Parauana (para1324), with reference records 581555 (Ramirez 2020), 665291 (Meira 2020), 143256 (Nowotny 1949), 154551 (Kann 1989), 546819 (Adelaar & Brijnen 2014).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Zero descriptive references. Comment: 'Parauana is an extinct Arawakan language attested by a wordlist in the re-discovered Natterer nachlass (Nowotny 1949, Kann 1989, Adelaar & Brijnen 2014). It has been shown by Ramirez 2020: 539-574 to be an independent language of the Negro-Roraima subgroup.' Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Ramirez, Henri & Maria Cristina Victorino de França. 2019. Línguas Arawak da Bolívia. LIAMES: Línguas Indígenas Americanas 19: e019012. DOI 10.20396/liames.v19i0.8655045.

sources.note: Nothing on Parawana stress. Names '†parawana' once (p. 2) among languages 'desenterradas há muito pouco tempo de manuscritos do século XIX' for the Enciclopédia; no Parawana data. Cites the primary as 'Natterer, Johann (s.d.). Wortlisten von Indianersprachen in Brasilien (1817-1835). Basileia: Basel University Library. (manuscrito)'.

sources.citation: Wikipedia (pt) 'Língua parawana' and Wikipedia (en) 'Parawana language', both citing Ramirez 2019 (preprint, p. 562) / 2020 vol. III (pp. 18, 36).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: pt page reproduces a ~65-item flora/fauna/artefact vocabulary 'coletado por Johann Natterer (1832)' as normalised by Ramirez; two items carry an acute accent (kamúü 'piraíba', tʃamé 'tabaco') with no explanation; no phonology or stress statement. en page is a stub (Parawana and Aroaqui 'may be the same language').

sources.citation: Adelaar, Willem F.H. & Hélène B. Brijnen. 2014. Johann Natterer and the Amazonian languages. Revista Brasileira de Linguística Antropológica 6(2): 333-352.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Silent on Parawana. Names 'Parahoana' once (p. 336) as one of three Natterer lists from the Brazil-Guyana savanna (with Atoraí and Wapishana). Pp. 339-340 discuss Natterer's diacritics in general: the acute accent on é marks vowel quality (central or mid front vowel), 'The motivation behind these different uses of é is not clear'; no stress interpretation for any language.

sources.note: The only linguistic treatment of the Natterer Parahoana list; Ramirez normally reconstructs a segment inventory for wordlist-only languages and may say how he read Natterer's accent marks (the acute accents on kamúü, tʃamé come from here). Best chance of any accent remark; a stress rule is unlikely for a 6-page wordlist language.
